variants.name: State as data members of the smallest owning class
variants.idiom_name: non-static data members of the owning class/struct; value semantics and RAII tie the state to the owner's lifetime
variants.implementation_notes: The default C++ realization: declare the state as non-static data members of the smallest class or struct that uses it - a widget's own class, a screen object, or a plain state struct owned by value. Lifetime is handled by the language: the members live inside the owner object and are destroyed with it (RAII), and copying or moving the owner moves the state with it. The replacement for the classic structure is exactly this ownership: where a shared record (namespace-scope variable or static data member) would be read by everything, the state now sits in the object that owns the behaviour. Namespace-scope and static data members remain justified only for genuinely process-wide state, and a shared editing value that several widgets observe belongs to the lowest common owner widget, not to a global.
pitfalls: A static data member or a namespace-scope variable is process-wide state with cross-translation-unit initialisation order problems - the C++ shape of the over-lifted store; keep it for genuine global state only.
Storing a reference or pointer to another object's member state outlives the owner if the owner is destroyed first; prefer ownership by value or a documented lifetime contract.
Copying the owner copies the state, so two copies can drift; delete or explicitly document copy/move semantics when the state is meant to be unique.

variants.name: Qt Quick component-local QML property with bindings
variants.idiom_name: custom property declared in the QML component that uses it; the QML engine re-evaluates bindings on change
variants.implementation_notes: In Qt Quick the colocated cell is a property declared in the object declaration itself: QML allows a component to declare its own property attributes, and such a property can maintain state internal to that object or expose it to the outside. Keep the property in the component whose behaviour uses it, derive everything derivable with binding expressions (the engine re-evaluates a binding when its dependencies change), and let parent components pass values down or accept signals up only for values that genuinely cross the component boundary. Lift to a shared model, a parent component or the C++ side when another component must read or control the value. This replaces the classic shared-state structure with per-component state plus binding, and is the right form when the UI is QML; keep the C++ data-member form when the widget tree is C++ or non-Qt.
pitfalls: Assigning a value imperatively to a property that has a binding removes the binding; keep the binding on derived properties and write only to the state property itself.
Properties belong to the object instance, so state is discarded when a delegate is re-created (for example after a model reset); use a model or a persistent owner for values that must survive.
QML ids are scoped to the component that declares them, so a child's state cannot be reached from outside - that is the intended encapsulation, but it surprises code that expects a global lookup.
